strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated and practically important problem (length bias / reward hacking in RLHF reward models), and the core idea—explicitly fitting the non-linear length–reward relation with a lightweight model, then penalizing the reward model's correlation with the fitted bias—is a sensible, well-specified extension over prior linear-assumption methods (ODIN, length penalty, Huang et al.).

The method is described in reasonable algorithmic detail (length encoding, ResNet fitting head, composite Pearson+MSE loss, alternating optimization schedule in Eq. 10–11), making the approach conceptually reproducible.

Evaluation goes beyond accuracy on preference data: it uses length-controlled Alpaca-Eval (LC-WR) under both BoN and DPO, reports output length statistics, and visualizes length–reward scatter and selected-response distributions, giving a multi-faceted view of debiasing.

The analysis of the fitted curve (multi-phase pattern: linear for short, sublinear for medium, noise-like for long responses) is an interesting empirical finding that partially explains why linear-assumption methods are inadequate and is a useful contribution in itself.

The paper is candid about trade-offs (e.g., the ~1–2 point drop in overall RM accuracy and the longer-than-ODIN outputs) and includes a thoughtful Limitations section acknowledging that length may legitimately correlate with quality.
weaknesses: Scale and breadth of evaluation are limited: a single dataset (Dahoas/rm-static from Anthropic HH), two Qwen2.5 model sizes, and no standard reward-model benchmark (e.g., RewardBench) or instruction-following suite beyond Alpaca-Eval. Generality of the claimed debiasing is therefore not well established.

Missing comparisons with directly relevant baselines: Singhal et al.'s length penalty, Shen et al.'s Product-of-Experts, Huang et al.'s post-hoc calibration, RRM, and WARM/WARP are discussed in related work but not empirically compared, so it is hard to attribute gains specifically to the non-linear fitting rather than to any regularization against length.

No statistical rigor: results appear to be single-run single-seed; no confidence intervals or significance tests for the LC-WR differences, which are modest (often ~1 point) and within plausible evaluation noise for a GPT-4-judged benchmark.

The DPO evaluation protocol is non-standard (relabeling the held-out set with each reward model rather than using the reward model in RL), which weakens the claim about downstream alignment; results under actual PPO/GRPO are absent, partly justified by computational cost.

No ablations: the contribution of the Pearson loss vs. MSE, the alternating schedule (a=8), the length-encoding design, and the number of fitting steps are not dissected; also, driving Pearson correlation of reward vs. r̂ toward zero does not provably remove all length dependence (e.g., higher-order or non-monotone components could remain).

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, and several details (fitting-model training steps, full hyperparameter set, exact Alpaca-Eval judge configuration, number of BoN samples per prompt, seeds) are unspecified.

Writing quality needs polishing: numerous typos and grammatical issues (e.g., 'socre', 'caculated', 'obversely', 'compare to', inconsistent capitalization in figures), and Eq. 11's indicator-function definition is confusingly presented for what is a simple alternating schedule.

The framing that prior work 'either does not characterize the bias form or assumes linearity' slightly oversimplifies the literature (e.g., ODIN's disentangled head and Huang et al.'s regression-based calibration also estimate the bias form), so the novelty claim is more incremental than stated.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and well-motivated problem: length bias in reward models, which is a documented cause of reward hacking and verbosity in RLHF-aligned LLMs.

The proposed method is clearly described and simple to follow: a lightweight length-encoding + ResNet fitting model learns the length-reward relation, which is then used to penalize correlation during reward model retraining.

Evaluation covers multiple downstream settings (BoN and reward-relabelled DPO) and two model scales (Qwen2.5-7B and 1.5B), using the length-controlled Alpaca-Eval metric, which is an appropriate choice for this problem.

The analysis of the fitted relation (approximately linear for short responses, sublinear for medium, noisy for long) is an interesting empirical observation, and the accuracy breakdown by C-longer/R-longer subsets is a thoughtful way to expose how apparent accuracy can mask length bias.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges that human preferences may genuinely correlate with length, which complicates the notion of 'debiasing'.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and a small delta over existing work: ODIN already decouples length from quality, and Huang et al. (2025) already performs post-hoc length-bias calibration; the core contribution amounts to replacing a linear/parametric bias form with a small MLP fit, which is a fairly incremental engineering change rather than a conceptual advance.

Narrow experimental scope: only one preference dataset (Dahoas/rm-static from Anthropic HH), one model family (Qwen2.5), and only two baselines (vanilla RM and ODIN). Important competing methods (length penalty, RRM, Shen et al., post-hoc calibration) are discussed but not compared.

Evaluation relies exclusively on GPT-4 as judge via Alpaca-Eval; no human evaluation is provided, and improvements are small (e.g., DPO 1.5B: LC-WR 73.84 vs 73.68 for vanilla RM, with lower raw WR). No variance estimates, seeds, or significance testing are reported, so it is hard to judge whether the gains are reliable.

Overall reward model accuracy drops notably (70.83 -> 69.00 for 7B), and the paper's defense of this trade-off is qualitative; a deeper analysis of what preference capability is lost (and whether debiasing to zero correlation is even desirable, given the acknowledged true length-quality correlation) is missing.

Missing ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity: no study of the loss components (Pearson vs MSE), the alternating-training scheme (a=8), embedding dimension, ResNet depth, or the number of alternating stages; the multi-phase 'finding' is based on a single fitted curve for one reward model, with no evidence of generality.

The DPO experiments use a non-standard setup (relabeling preference data with each reward model rather than standard DPO training), which limits comparability with prior DPO-based length-bias work and makes the reported gains harder to interpret.

Reproducibility is weak: no code release is mentioned, and key details are missing (DPO beta, number of evaluation prompts, judge configuration, exact binning procedure). Many quantitative claims are supported only by qualitative scatter/density plots.

Writing quality needs improvement: numerous typos and grammatical issues ('socre', 'caculated', 'obversely', 'could validating', 'strengthen the regulatory'), imprecise phrasing, and an oddly abrupt societal-impact paragraph in the conclusion.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: length bias in reward models, a widely documented form of reward hacking in RLHF.

The core idea is clearly articulated: rather than assuming a linear length-reward relation (as in ODIN, length penalty, or Huang et al.'s linear regression), a lightweight fitting model learns the bias form non-parametrically and this learned relation is used to debias the reward model.

The three-stage framework (warm-up, bias fitting, debiasing) is described in enough algorithmic and hyperparameter detail (losses, LE encoding, alternating training schedule, batch sizes, learning rates) to be reasonably reproducible.

Evaluation covers multiple angles: per-subset preference accuracy (C-longer/R-longer), length-reward scatter plots, BoN and DPO downstream results with length-controlled Alpaca-Eval, and qualitative analysis of selection-length distributions.

The analysis of the fitted curve (linear for short responses, sublinear for medium, noise-like for long) is an interesting empirical observation that partially validates and partially refutes the linear assumptions of prior work, and is a useful contribution beyond the method itself.
The Limitations section is honest, correctly noting that length is not necessarily orthogonal to true human preference quality.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are small and inconsistent. In DPO for Qwen2.5-1.5B, the vanilla RM actually achieves the highest raw win rate (79.67 vs. 79.41) and LC-WR differences are within a fraction of a point. No significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance over GPT-4-judge runs is reported, so many of the headline improvements cannot be confidently distinguished from noise.

Overall reward model accuracy drops noticeably (e.g., 70.83 -> 69.00 for 7B, 70.65 -> 68.00 for 1.5B). The paper argues the drop reflects rebalancing across length subsets, but the trade-off between debiasing and preference-modeling capability is not analyzed in depth (e.g., is the lost accuracy on genuinely high-quality pairs?).

Missing comparisons against important baselines: no results for the simple length penalty of Singhal et al. [41], Product-of-Experts (Shen et al. [40]), RRM, or Huang et al. [19]. Since the central claim is that non-linear fitting beats linear assumption, a direct apples-to-apples comparison with a linear regression baseline or even simple polynomial/spline regression on the same pipeline is essential and absent.

Novelty is modest: the method amounts to fitting a small MLP (length encoding + two-layer ResNet) to a scalar function of length and penalizing its correlation with reward outputs. The technical machinery is simple; the contribution rests mostly on the empirical characterization and the application, which limits main-conference-level impact.

The key 'multiphase bias pattern' finding is derived from a single fit on one dataset (Dahoas rm-static / Anthropic HH) with one model family (Qwen2.5). No verification across datasets, model families, or reward model scales is provided, so the generality of the claimed bias structure is uncertain.

The DPO evaluation protocol is non-standard: human preference labels are replaced by reward-model re-annotations before DPO training, which entangles reward-model quality with the alignment result and complicates interpretation.
No PPO experiments despite RLHF being the stated target; only BoN (N=8) and a relabeled DPO variant are evaluated.

Writing quality needs substantial polishing: repeated grammatical and typographical errors ('socre', 'caculated', 'obversely', 'Our contributions can summarized', 'which could validating', 'These algorithms represent different approaches' with awkward constructions), inconsistent notation and citation formatting.
No code release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility despite the reasonable methodological detail.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: length bias in reward models is a recognized form of reward hacking, and the paper's core idea—learning the length-reward bias function with a lightweight fitting model rather than assuming linearity—is a reasonable and cleanly executed refinement of prior work (Length Penalty, ODIN, Huang et al. 2025).

Comprehensive empirical validation: two base models (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B), multiple alignment algorithms (BoN, DPO, plus SimPO and GRPO in the appendix), two preference datasets (Dahoas-rm-static, RLHFlow), and multiple evaluation angles (preference accuracy on C-longer/R-longer splits, length-reward scatter plots, LC-WR/WR, MT-Bench, IFEval, selection-length distributions).

Thoughtful analysis of the accuracy trade-off on preference subsets: the authors correctly argue that a length-biased RM inflates C-longer accuracy (58% of the data) and that the balanced accuracy profile is evidence of debiasing rather than degradation.
Useful ablations (joint vs. multi-stage training, alternating schedule, four alternative fitting architectures) and a transparent computational cost analysis showing the method adds no overhead.

Honest Limitations section acknowledging that human preferences are not fully independent of length and that forcing zero correlation may be over-correction; the empirical finding of a piecewise (linear-then-flattening) bias curve is a mildly interesting contribution.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: the method is essentially a non-linear extension of existing post-hoc length calibration (Huang et al. 2025, linear regression) combined with a Pearson-based decorrelation objective. The delta over prior work is small, and the ablations undercut the headline claim—'Linear Fitting' achieves 71.67 LC-WR vs. 72.59 for the full method, a modest gap, while polynomial regression performs anomalously poorly (67.11), suggesting fragility rather than a robust advantage of the learned non-linearity.

Evaluation circularity in the DPO experiments: preference labels are replaced by reward model predictions, so the aligned model largely distills the reward model being evaluated. The downstream gains (Tables 3, 4) partly measure the debiased RM's agreement with itself rather than genuine quality, and this is not discussed.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting anywhere: differences on MT-Bench/IFEval (e.g., 4.82 vs. 4.53 Avg; 19.0 vs. 18.6 prompt accuracy) and several LC-WR margins are small relative to plausible run-to-run and LLM-judge variance, yet no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are provided.

Training and evaluation rely on a small, single-domain static dataset (Dahoas-rm-static, ~30k pairs) for the main results; RLHFlow appears only in an appendix with a vanilla-RM-only comparison, so generality to realistic modern preference data is under-supported.

The Pearson-based objective enforces zero linear correlation per batch, not independence, and batch-size-sensitive correlation estimates (mitigated only by multi-GPU aggregation) could make debiasing noisy; the interaction of L'pearson with LBT (e.g., weighting of the two terms) is not analyzed.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters.

Presentation issues: several writing errors ('Therefore, we must strengthen the regulatory', 'assume a approximate linear relation', 'it fails to capture some details'), garbled Figure 1 rendering, and the fitted-curve analysis (Figure 7) is descriptive only—the fitted model is never validated out-of-sample or compared quantitatively against the true bias function.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (length bias in reward models) and the proposed FiMi-RM framework is clearly motivated and described in reasonable technical detail, including the fitting model architecture (Sec. 3.2, App. C), alternating training schedule (Eq. 7-8), and loss design.

The empirical evaluation is broad for a paper of this scope: two base model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B), multiple alignment algorithms (BoN, DPO, SimPO, GRPO), several metrics (LC-WR, WR, length statistics), and additional benchmarks (MT-Bench, IFEval), with appendices covering a second dataset (RLHFlow).

Useful supporting analyses are provided: ablations over the training schedule and fitting-model architecture (Table 5), a computational cost analysis showing no training-time overhead (Table 7), BT-loss monitoring during debiasing (App. E), and visualization of the fitted length-reward curve at different training steps (Fig. 7).

The paper is commendably honest about a key limitation: forcing zero length-reward correlation may discard genuine length-quality correlation in human preferences, and it discusses this explicitly in the Limitations section.
weaknesses: The headline claim that non-linear bias fitting is essential is not well supported by the paper's own evidence: the linear-fitting ablation achieves 71.67 LC-WR vs. 72.59 for the full ResNet-based fitter (Table 5), a gap of under one point that is never tested for significance. This undercuts the central motivation that moving beyond linear relations yields substantial gains.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported anywhere, despite many reported improvements being small (e.g., preference accuracy 69.75 vs. 70.14; MT-Bench 4.82 vs. 4.53). Given the noise inherent in GPT-4-judged Alpaca-Eval evaluation, the reliability of the improvements is uncertain.

Novelty is limited and the delta over prior work is modest. The idea of learning a scalar length-to-reward mapping and subtracting/decoupling it is very close to ODIN (two-head disentangling), Huang et al. (2025) post-hoc reward calibration, and Singhal et al. (2023) length penalty; the contribution essentially replaces a linear/parametric form with a tiny (6.4K-parameter) MLP regression, and the Pearson-correlation loss is an unusual and arguably over-engineered substitute for a direct 1-D regression on binned reward-length data, which is never compared against.

The DPO evaluation setup is nonstandard and potentially circular: human preference labels are replaced by labels assigned by the reward model itself (Sec. 4.1), so downstream DPO results partly measure agreement with the (debiased) reward model rather than genuine alignment quality.

Experiments are confined to a single small static dataset (Dahoas rm-static) with short responses (mostly under ~300 tokens) in the main results; the generality of the fitted non-linear bias pattern to realistic, longer-response preference data is not established, and the fitted curve's flattening beyond 100 tokens (Fig. 7) is presented descriptively without analysis of whether it is a genuine property of the bias or an artifact.

Some evidence is qualitative: Figure 2's y-axis is deliberately unlabeled and 'more balanced distribution' claims rest on visual inspection of scatter plots and histograms; Figure 3/4 density differences are small and unquantified.

Writing quality is below the bar for submission, with recurring grammatical errors ('Previous approaches operating under the assumption... so they could', 'are typically not characterize', 'Huang et.al.', 'we must strengthen the regulatory'), which impairs clarity. No code or artifact release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the full pipeline.

The large GRPO improvement (LC-WR 58.80 to 67.42, Table 10) appears only against the vanilla baseline with no comparison to ODIN or Length Penalty, making it hard to contextualize and raising questions about what drives the gain.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and relevant problem (length bias in reward models for RLHF), with a clearly articulated limitation of prior work (either not characterizing bias form, or assuming linear length-reward relations).

The proposed FiMi-RM method is simple, lightweight (~6.4K-parameter fitting model), and well specified: the three-stage pipeline, Pearson-correlation-based losses with stop-gradient variants, and the alternating training schedule (Eq. 7-8) are all clearly defined.

The empirical analysis of the fitted bias curve (Figure 7) is genuinely informative: the two-phase pattern (strong linear relation under 100 tokens, flattening/slight downward trend beyond) provides concrete evidence that the linear assumption of prior work is incomplete, which is the paper's central scientific claim.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: two base models (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B), multiple alignment algorithms (BoN, DPO, SimPO, GRPO), length-controlled AlpacaEval plus MT-Bench and IFEval, multiple analyses of length-reward and length-selection distributions, and a second training dataset (RLHFlow).

Ablations (Appendix A) directly test the design choices: joint vs. staged training, alternating updates, and five fitting-model architectures; the linear-fitting variant (71.67 vs. 72.59 LC-WR) gives some support for the nonlinearity claim, and the ablation table is reported honestly (polynomial regression underperforms).

Computational cost is analyzed transparently (Table 7), showing debiasing comes with no net training-time overhead, and the Bradley-Terry loss increase during Stage 3 is monitored and explained (Appendix E).
Limitations are candidly discussed, including the open question of whether length and true preference are truly independent.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method is a close relative of ODIN (disentangling length and quality) and Huang et al. (2025) post-hoc reward calibration; the main delta is a learned non-linear bias model trained jointly with the reward model. The comparison with Huang et al. is textual rather than experimental.

The evidence that nonlinearity is crucial is not fully convincing: the linear-fitting ablation trails the full method by only ~0.9 LC-WR, and the polynomial regression variant performs much worse than even the linear one, which is unexplained and hints at optimization/initialization issues rather than expressive power alone.

No statistical rigor: results are single runs with no seeds, variance estimates, or significance tests, while many headline gaps (e.g., 72.59 vs. 71.38 LC-WR) are within plausible run-to-run variation. GPT-4-judged AlpacaEval is also a noisy primary metric.

Baseline coverage is thin: only Length Penalty and ODIN are compared; several directly relevant length-debiasing methods (Shen et al. PoE, ALBM, RRM, Park et al.'s DPO length regularization) are discussed but not benchmarked.

A potentially important confound is under-analyzed: a debiased RM that prefers shorter responses could simply be trading quality for conciseness; the paper argues against this via LC-WR but the mechanism by which debiasing improves WR on MT-Bench/IFEval (Table 4) is not explained, and some reported MT-Bench/IFEval absolute scores are quite low.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is stated, and several hyperparameters (fitting model learning rate schedule, warm-up step counts beyond Table 7, debiasing loss weighting) would need clarification; the Pearson loss's dependence on large batch statistics adds implementation subtlety.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., 'Reward model (modelr...)', grammatical slips like 'reduces accuracy on the C-longer subset while improving it on R-longer' needs the clarification it eventually gets later), and Figure 1's rendering is hard to parse in places.
